title: B2+ · L46 — Productivity vocabulary
description: Vocabulario moderno de productividad: deep work, batching, deliverables, async, focus blocks, context switching.

questions.prompt: Tu manager te pregunta como estructuras tus mananas.
questions.question: 'Deep work' means:
options: Focused, distraction-free cognitive work on demanding tasks.
questions.explanation: Deep work (termino de Cal Newport) = trabajo cognitivo intenso sin distracciones. Contrasta con 'shallow work' (emails, admin). En reuniones y roadmaps es un termino cotidiano. NO confundir con 'hard work' generico.
examples: I block off two hours of deep work every morning before Slack. → rutina de senior IC
This problem needs deep work, not another quick sync. → pushback contra meeting overload

questions.question: A 'deliverable' is:
options: A concrete output or artifact promised by a deadline.
questions.explanation: Deliverable = output tangible que se entrega al final de una fase (doc, prototype, report, release). Vocabulario estandar de PMs y consulting. Distintos de 'tasks' (steps) o 'milestones' (fechas clave).
examples: The Q3 deliverables are the design spec and a working prototype.
Let's align on deliverables before we scope the timeline. → planning con cliente

questions.statement: 'Batching' tasks means grouping similar tasks together to reduce context switching.
questions.explanation: Batching = agrupar tareas similares (todos los emails a las 4pm, todos los code reviews un bloque). Reduce el coste de 'context switching' (cambiar de tipo de trabajo). Tecnica core de productividad moderna.
examples: I batch all my one-on-ones on Tuesdays to protect the rest of the week.
Batching invoices at month-end saves me hours. → ejemplo freelancer

questions.prompt: Colega se queja: 'I can't get anything done, I keep jumping between Slack, email, and code.'
questions.question: The problem she's describing is:
questions.explanation: Context switching = coste cognitivo de alternar entre tareas de distinto tipo. Cada switch cuesta ~15-25 min recuperar focus. 'Multitasking' es el mito; 'context switching' es la realidad. Es el villano de la productividad de knowledge workers.
examples: Context switching kills my flow — I need 90-minute blocks.
Every Slack ping is a context switch in disguise. → queja tipica de dev

questions.text: I've started blocking off two-hour focus sessions in the morning and defending them ruthlessly against meetings.
questions.explanation: Discurso de knowledge worker senior. 'Blocking off' (phrasal verb reservar) y 'defending them ruthlessly' — colocacion muy natural. Nota el linking: 'two-hour' se pronuncia 'two-wow-er', y 'defending them' funde la /d/ con la /th/.
examples: Focus sessions only work if you defend them from meetings.
I block off Wednesdays entirely — no calls, just deep work.

questions.question: 'Async' (short for asynchronous) work means:
questions.explanation: Async = comunicacion que NO requiere respuesta inmediata (docs, Loom, threads, Notion). Contrasta con 'sync' (meetings, calls). Default en teams remote/globales. 'Async-first' es filosofia de empresas como GitLab.
examples: We're async-first — meetings are a last resort.
Post it in the channel async so the EU team can read it tomorrow. → workflow global

questions.prompt: Empareja cada tecnica/concepto de productividad con su definicion:

pairs.right: Agrupar tareas similares en un bloque
Reservar bloques en el calendario por actividad
Coste de cambiar entre tareas dispares
Output tangible con fecha de entrega

questions.explanation: Todos son terminos operacionales de knowledge work moderno. 'Time-blocking' (Cal Newport) es implementacion practica de deep work + batching. 'Backlog' viene de agile pero se usa en cualquier funcion.
examples: My calendar is time-blocked by activity type, not by meetings.
The backlog has 40 items — we need to ruthlessly prioritize.

questions.target: I try to protect my mornings for deep work and batch all the shallow stuff — emails, reviews, admin — into a single afternoon block.
questions.explanation: Discurso de knowledge worker senior explicando su sistema. Nota 'protect my mornings', 'batch all the shallow stuff', 'single afternoon block' — colocaciones autenticas. La estructura contrasta deep vs shallow, muy comun en podcasts de productividad.
examples: Mornings are for deep work, afternoons for shallow stuff and meetings.
I batch admin into one block so it doesn't leak into the whole day. → founder discipline

questions.prompt: Manager review: 'You have great output but the quality is uneven.'
questions.question: 'Output' in a work context means:
questions.explanation: Output = cantidad/volumen de trabajo producido. Se contrasta con 'outcome' (impacto real). Manager sofisticado dira: 'Focus on outcomes, not just output' — mucho trabajo no equivale a impacto. Palabra clave en performance reviews.
examples: High output, but we need to measure outcomes too.
Her output dropped this quarter but each deliverable is sharper. → matiz maduro

questions.statement: 'Bandwidth' in a work context refers to internet speed only.
questions.explanation: FALSO. 'Bandwidth' se usa metaforicamente para 'capacidad mental/tiempo disponible'. 'I don't have the bandwidth this week' es forma profesional (y comun) de decir no. Se dice tanto o mas en oficina que en contexto tecnico.
examples: I don't have the bandwidth to take on another project this sprint. → decline diplomatico
Do you have bandwidth for a 20-minute review today? → pregunta educada

questions.question: Complete: 'Mondays are ___ — back-to-back meetings and no time to think.'
questions.explanation: 'Brutal' es la colocacion informal-profesional estandar para describir una semana/dia muy dificil. 'A breeze' es opuesto (facil). 'Shallow' describe el tipo de trabajo, no la dificultad del dia. 'Deep' se aplica a work, no a dia.
examples: This week is brutal — I'm in meetings until 7 every day.
The launch week was brutal but we shipped. → tono founder normal

questions.text: Honestly, we need to cut the meetings by half and move everything else to async docs and Loom videos.
questions.explanation: Discurso muy natural con discourse marker inicial ('Honestly'). 'Cut the meetings by half' (colocacion practica), 'move everything else to async' (uso moderno). En hablado 'need to' se contrae a 'need-tuh' y 'everything' pierde la 'h'.
examples: We should cut the recurring meetings by half — most are async-able.
Loom-first, meeting-only-if-needed is our new default. → policy anuncio

questions.prompt: PM defiende su decision en un review.
questions.question: 'Prioritization' at senior level means:
options: Deciding what NOT to do so you can go deep on what matters.
questions.explanation: En senior level, prioritization = decidir que NO hacer. 'The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do' (Porter). Junior confunde priorizar con ordenar; senior sabe que es cortar. Frase clave en 1:1s: 'What are we saying no to?'
examples: Real prioritization means saying no to good ideas, not just bad ones.
What are we explicitly NOT doing this quarter? → pregunta senior en planning

questions.statement: 'To 'get in the zone'' means to enter a state of deep focus and flow.
questions.explanation: 'Get in the zone' = entrar en estado de flow. Sinonimos: 'be in flow', 'get in flow state'. Muy usado por developers, writers, athletes. Preserva 'the' — 'get in zone' suena mal.
examples: Once I'm in the zone, an hour feels like ten minutes.
Music with no lyrics helps me get in the zone faster. → dev habit

questions.target: Look, if we don't cut this backlog in half, we're going to burn out the team — we need fewer priorities, not more people.
questions.explanation: Discurso de manager senior en un tough conversation. 'Look' (discourse marker que precede a argumento fuerte), 'cut this backlog in half' (colocacion), 'burn out the team' (phrasal noun), y el paralelismo final 'fewer priorities, not more people' — retorica de eng leader mature.
examples: We don't have a resourcing problem — we have a prioritization problem.
Hiring won't fix this; ruthless prioritization will. → argumento contra scaling ciego
